messages.subject: grouping of heaped data
parts:

Another question for the list. Concerning grouping of data to reduce the e=
ffects of heaping, can someone please explain to me the general method of=
doing this in Distance? I'm not sure when I'm selecting my group cut-po=
ints if I'm aiming for the best fit of the groups to the detection functi=

In some cases, when I have a very low Chi-square value for my first interva=

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: grouping of heaped data
parts:
> > Another question for the list. Concerning grouping of data to reduce the effects of heaping, can someone please explain to me the general method of doing this in Distance? I'm not sure when I'm selecting my group cut-points if I'm aiming for the best fit of the groups to the detection function of an arbitrarily picked model, or if I should be using the GOF test values for the cutpoints to obtain groupings that have the lowest Chi-square value?
> >
> > In some cases, when I have a very low Chi-square value for my first interval, the group has a detection probability that is not very close to 1 (ie. 0.85, 0.9). In other cases, I will have a first interval group that has a detection probability very close to 1, however the chi-square value for that interval is higher than the former example.
> >
> > How does one decide what the best grouping is to reduce the effects of heaping? I can't seem to find a definitive answer in the manual/book.

I would not choose intervals with reference to goodness-of-fit statistics
- though a good choice of groups should improve the reliability of gof
tests. I would examine the data, and the behaviour of my observers, to
determine what the favoured rounding distances are. I would then choose
cutpoints to try to ensure that these favoured distances fall well away
from cutpoints. In this way, few observations should end up in the wrong
group.

If heaping is substantial, I would also look to improve field methods and
observer training, and assess whether technology such as survey lasers can
reduce the problem of heaping.

Steve Buckland
